title: Simple Linear Regression and Correlation
summary: Many problems involve the relationship between two or more variables: the strength of a weld and its temperature, the fuel use of a car and its weight. An empirical model is an equation fitted to observed data that describes this relationship without being…

blocks.x: Many problems involve the relationship between two or more variables: the strength of a weld and its temperature, the fuel use of a car and its weight. An empirical model is an equation fitted to observed data that describes this relationship without being derived from first principles. Typically the response $Y$ is random and the regressor $x$ is a quantity whose value we choose or measure with negligible error.
The simple linear regression model is
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\varepsilon,

where $\beta_0$ (the intercept) and $\beta_1$ (the slope) are unknown regression coefficients and $\varepsilon$ is a random error with $\Exp[\varepsilon]=0$ and $\Var[\varepsilon]=\sigma^2$. For data $(x_i,y_i)$, $i=1,\dots,n$: $Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i$ with the $\varepsilon_i$ independent. For inference we also assume the errors are normal, $\varepsilon_i\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2)$.

Then for fixed $x$, $\Exp(Y\mid x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x$ (the mean response lies on a straight line), $\Var(Y\mid x)=\sigma^2$ (constant variance), and $\beta_1$ is the change in the mean response per unit change in $x$.
Throughout this chapter we use the following $n=8$ observations.

blocks.caption: The least squares line minimises the sum of squared vertical distances (dashed) from the data points to the line.

blocks.x: The method of least squares
We estimate $\beta_0,\beta_1$ by choosing the line that makes the data as close as possible, in the sense of minimising the sum of squared vertical deviations
L(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i\big)^2.
Setting $\partial L/\partial\beta_0=0$ and $\partial L/\partial\beta_1=0$ gives the least squares normal equations
n\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\sum x_i=\sum y_i,\qquad\hat\beta_0\sum x_i+\hat\beta_1\sum x_i^2=\sum x_iy_i.
$S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2=\sum x_i^2-\dfrac{(\sum x_i)^2}n$, $\ S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})=\sum x_iy_i-\dfrac{(\sum x_i)(\sum y_i)}n$, and $S_{yy}=\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2$.
\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}-\hat\beta_1\bar{x}.
The fitted line is $\hat{y}=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x$ and the residuals are $e_i=y_i-\hat{y}_i$. The line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$.

The first normal equation gives $\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}-\hat\beta_1\bar{x}$. Substituting into the second: $\hat\beta_1\big(\sum x_i^2-n\bar{x}^2\big)=\sum x_iy_i-n\bar{x}\bar{y}$, i.e. $\hat\beta_1S_{xx}=S_{xy}$. The second derivatives show that this is a minimum ($L$ is a convex quadratic).
Estimating $\sigma^2$
The error variance is estimated from the residuals.
$SS_E=\sum_{i=1}^ne_i^2=\sum(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2$, and
\hat\sigma^2=MS_E=\frac{SS_E}{n-2}.
A convenient computing formula is $SS_E=S_{yy}-\hat\beta_1S_{xy}$.

The divisor $n-2$ is the degrees of freedom: two parameters ($\beta_0,\beta_1$) were estimated from the data, so two degrees of freedom are lost, and with it $\Exp[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2$ (shown below). In Example 5.5: $SS_E=167.795-1.9976(83.9)=0.195$ and $\hat\sigma^2=0.195/6=0.0325$, so $\hat\sigma=0.180$.

sections.title: Properties of the Least Squares Estimators

blocks.x: Write $\hat\beta_1=\sum c_iY_i$ with $c_i=(x_i-\bar{x})/S_{xx}$; the $x_i$ are fixed, so $\hat\beta_1$ is a linear combination of the independent $Y_i$.
Under the model assumptions:
$\Exp[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1$ and $\Var[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$;
$\Exp[\hat\beta_0]=\beta_0$ and $\Var[\hat\beta_0]=\sigma^2\Big(\dfrac1n+\dfrac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\Big)$;
$\Exp[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2$;
if the errors are normal, $\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1$ are normal, and $(n-2)\hat\sigma^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-2}$ independently of $(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)$.
The estimated standard errors are $\se(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}$ and $\se(\hat\beta_0)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2(1/n+\bar{x}^2/S_{xx})}$.

(i) Since $\sum c_i=0$ and $\sum c_ix_i=1$: $\Exp[\hat\beta_1]=\sum c_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)=\beta_1$, and $\Var[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2\sum c_i^2=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$. (ii) $\hat\beta_0=\bar{Y}-\hat\beta_1\bar{x}$; the terms $\bar{Y}$ and $\hat\beta_1$ are uncorrelated (because $\sum c_i=0$), so $\Var[\hat\beta_0]=\sigma^2/n+\bar{x}^2\sigma^2/S_{xx}$. (iii) and (iv) are proved in the matrix setting in Chapter 6 (Theorem 6.8): the residual vector lies in an $(n-2)$-dimensional space.

Among all linear unbiased estimators of $\beta_1$ (estimators of the form $\sum a_iY_i$), $\hat\beta_1$ has the smallest variance; likewise for $\hat\beta_0$. The least squares estimators are the best linear unbiased estimators (BLUE), requiring only uncorrelated errors with equal variance, not normality.

$\Var[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$ shrinks when the noise $\sigma$ is small, when $n$ is large, and when the $x$-values are spread out (large $S_{xx}$). A designed experiment should place regressor values at the extremes of the range: half at each end maximises $S_{xx}$ for given $n$ and range (though it cannot detect curvature, so a few middle points are added). Extrapolating beyond the range of the data is dangerous, since the fitted line says nothing about whether the relationship stays linear there.

sections.title: Some Comments on Uses of Regression (CD Only)

blocks.x: Regression is used for description (summarising a trend), prediction (estimating the response at a new $x$ within the range of the data) and control (choosing $x$ to achieve a target $y$). Cautions: (1) a fitted line is valid only in the region of the observed $x$, (2) a strong fit shows association, not causation, (3) the regression of $y$ on $x$ is not the regression of $x$ on $y$ (the two lines differ unless the correlation is $\pm1$), (4) the model assumes $x$ is measured without error, and (5) a few influential points can control the whole fit.

sections.title: Hypothesis Tests in Simple Linear Regression

blocks.x: Use of $t$-Tests
With normal errors, standardising each coefficient with its estimated standard error gives a $t$ statistic.

$T=\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-\beta_{1,0}}{\se(\hat\beta_1)}\sim t_{n-2}$ when $\beta_1=\beta_{1,0}$, and similarly $T=\dfrac{\hat\beta_0-\beta_{0,0}}{\se(\hat\beta_0)}\sim t_{n-2}$. To test $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_{1,0}$ against $H_1:\beta_1\ne\beta_{1,0}$, reject if $\abs{t_0}>t_{\alpha/2,n-2}$.

The most important special case is $H_0:\beta_1=0$ against $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$, the test for significance of regression. Failing to reject means there is no evidence of a linear relationship between $x$ and $Y$ (either $x$ is of little value in explaining $Y$, or the true relationship is not linear); rejecting means $x$ is useful in explaining $Y$ (the line is a better model than a constant, though a curve might be better still).

For Example 5.5: $\se(\hat\beta_1)=\sqrt{0.0325/42}=0.0278$ and $t_0=1.9976/0.0278=71.8$ with $6$ degrees of freedom, far beyond $t_{0.005,6}=3.707$: reject $H_0:\beta_1=0$ ($P<0.0001$). For the intercept, $\se(\hat\beta_0)=\sqrt{0.0325(1/8+20.25/42)}=0.1405$ and $t_0=0.0357/0.1405=0.25$: no evidence that the intercept differs from $0$.

Reading the test of $H_0:\beta_1=0$ (significance of regression). Failing to reject $H_0$ means either that $x$ is of little value in explaining $Y$ (the best estimate of $Y$ for every $x$ is $\bar{y}$) or that the true relationship is not linear. Rejecting $H_0$ means that $x$ explains variability in $Y$, which can mean either that the straight line is adequate or that the line is a good first approximation and a higher-order term would do better. Also $\hat\beta_0$ and $\hat\beta_1$ are not independent: $\operatorname{cov}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)=-\bar{x}\sigma^2/S_{xx}$.

Oxygen purity $y$ (%) against hydrocarbon level $x$ (%), $n=20$: $S_{xx}=0.68088$, $S_{xy}=10.17744$, so $\hat\beta_1=14.947$ and $\hat\beta_0=74.283$, giving $\hat{y}=74.283+14.947x$. The predicted purity at $x=1.00$ is $89.23\%$. $SS_T=173.38$, $SS_R=\hat\beta_1S_{xy}=152.13$, $SS_E=21.25$ and $\hat\sigma^2=1.18$. To test $H_0:\beta_1=0$ at $\alpha=0.01$: $t_0=11.35$ against $t_{0.005,18}=2.88$, and $F_0=152.13/1.18=128.86$ ($=t_0^2$), $P\approx1.2\times10^{-9}$: reject. $R^2=152.13/173.38=0.877$, so the model accounts for $87.7\%$ of the variability.
Analysis of Variance Approach to Test Significance of Regression
The total variability of the responses splits into a part explained by the regression and a part left over.
\underbrace{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2}_{SS_T=S_{yy}}=\underbrace{\sum(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})^2}_{SS_R=\hat\beta_1S_{xy}}+\underbrace{\sum(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}_{SS_E},
with degrees of freedom $n-1=1+(n-2)$.

Write $y_i-\bar{y}=(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})+(y_i-\hat{y}_i)$ and square; the cross term is $2\sum(\hat{y}_i-\bar{y})e_i=2\hat\beta_1\sum(x_i-\bar{x})e_i=0$, because the normal equations make the residuals sum to zero and orthogonal to the $x_i$.
The ratio of mean squares gives an $F$ test equivalent to the $t$-test.

Let $MS_R=SS_R/1$ and $MS_E=SS_E/(n-2)$. Under $H_0:\beta_1=0$, $F_0=MS_R/MS_E\sim F_{1,n-2}$, and $H_0$ is rejected if $f_0>f_{\alpha,1,n-2}$. Moreover $F_0=T_0^2$, where $T_0=\hat\beta_1/\se(\hat\beta_1)$.
Confidence Intervals on the Slope and Intercept

A two-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval on $\beta_1$ is $\hat\beta_1\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}$, and on $\beta_0$ is $\hat\beta_0\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2(1/n+\bar{x}^2/S_{xx})}$. A confidence interval on $\sigma^2$ is $\dfrac{(n-2)\hat\sigma^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-2}}\le\sigma^2\le\dfrac{(n-2)\hat\sigma^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}}$.

One-sided versions use $\alpha$ in a single tail and write one limit only: upper bound $\beta_1\le\hat\beta_1+t_{\alpha,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}$, lower bound $\hat\beta_1-t_{\alpha,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2/S_{xx}}\le\beta_1$ (similarly for $\beta_0$), and $\sigma^2\le(n-2)\hat\sigma^2/\chi^2_{1-\alpha,n-2}$, $\sigma^2\ge(n-2)\hat\sigma^2/\chi^2_{\alpha,n-2}$. The matching tests reject $H_1:\beta_1>\beta_{1,0}$ when $t_0>t_{\alpha,n-2}$ and $H_1:\beta_1<\beta_{1,0}$ when $t_0<-t_{\alpha,n-2}$. The end of a two-sided $95\%$ interval is a one-sided $97.5\%$ bound, not a one-sided $95\%$ bound. The same applies to the interval on $\mu_{Y|x_0}$ and the prediction interval below: replace $t_{\alpha/2,n-2}$ by $t_{\alpha,n-2}$ and keep one limit.
Confidence Interval on the Mean Response

The mean response at $x=x_0$ is $\mu_{Y|x_0}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0$, estimated by $\hat\mu_{Y|x_0}=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0$, which is normal and unbiased with variance $\sigma^2\Big[\dfrac1n+\dfrac{(x_0-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}\Big]$.
A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval on $\mu_{Y|x_0}$ is
\hat\mu_{Y|x_0}\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\Big[\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}\Big]}.
The interval is narrowest at $x_0=\bar{x}$ and widens as $x_0$ moves away from the centre of the data: our knowledge of the line is best in the middle.
A new individual observation $Y_0$ at $x_0$ equals the mean response plus a new error $\varepsilon_0$ independent of the data.
A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ prediction interval for a future observation $Y_0$ at $x_0$ is
\hat{y}_0\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-2}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\Big[1+\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}}\Big]}.
$Y_0-\hat{Y}_0$ has mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2+\sigma^2[1/n+(x_0-\bar{x})^2/S_{xx}]$ (the two parts are independent), and standardising with $\hat\sigma$ gives a $t_{n-2}$ pivot.

At $x_0=5$: $\sqrt{0.0325(1+0.1310)}=0.1917$, so the prediction interval is $10.024\pm2.447(0.1917)=10.024\pm0.469$, much wider than the interval $\pm0.160$ for the mean response: even with the line known exactly, a single new observation still scatters by $\sigma$.
The tests and intervals are valid only if the model assumptions hold: linearity, independent errors with constant variance and (for small $n$) normality.
Residual Analysis

$e_i=y_i-\hat{y}_i$. The standardised residuals are $d_i=e_i/\hat\sigma$; about $95\%$ of them should lie within $\pm2$ if the model is correct. A point far outside is a potential outlier, but outliers can carry important information and should not be discarded automatically. The $t$-test of $H_0:\beta_1=0$ is more flexible than the $F$-test because it also allows one-sided alternatives.
Graphical checks:
Normal probability plot of residuals: points near a straight line support normality; curvature indicates skew or heavy tails.

Residuals versus fitted values (or versus $x$): a random horizontal band is good; a curved pattern means the straight line is the wrong shape (try a quadratic term or a transformation); a funnel (spread increasing with $\hat{y}$) indicates non-constant variance (try a variance-stabilising transformation of the response, $\sqrt{y}$, $\ln y$ or $1/y$, or weighted least squares).
Residuals versus time order: runs of same-sign residuals indicate correlated errors.
Coefficient of Determination ($R^2$)
$R^2=\dfrac{SS_R}{SS_T}=1-\dfrac{SS_E}{SS_T}$, the proportion of the variability in $y$ explained by the regression, with $0\le R^2\le1$.

For the data above $R^2=167.600/167.795=0.9988$. Cautions: $R^2$ does not measure the size of the slope (a large $R^2$ does not mean a steep line) nor the appropriateness of the model (adding polynomial terms can inflate it, and it can be large even when the relationship is nonlinear); you can reach $R^2=1$ by fitting a polynomial of degree $n-1$. Further: a large $R^2$ does not prove that the linear model is correct (a curved relationship over a limited range can give $R^2$ near $1$), and a small $R^2$ is not necessarily a bad model if the noise is naturally large. $R^2$ never decreases when regressors are added, so it cannot be used to compare models with different numbers of regressors (see Chapter 6).
Lack-of-Fit Test (CD Only)
If there are repeated observations at some values of $x$ (replicates), the error sum of squares can be split into pure error (variation among replicates) and lack of fit:
SS_E=SS_{PE}+SS_{LOF},\qquad SS_{PE}=\sum_i\sum_j(y_{ij}-\bar{y}_i)^2\ (n-m\text{ df}),\quad SS_{LOF}=SS_E-SS_{PE}\ (m-2\text{ df}),

where $m$ is the number of distinct $x$-values. Under the hypothesis that the straight line is adequate, $F_0=\dfrac{SS_{LOF}/(m-2)}{SS_{PE}/(n-m)}\sim F_{m-2,n-m}$; a large $F_0$ is evidence of curvature.
If a scatter plot is clearly curved, a transformation of $x$, $y$ or both may make the relationship linear, after which the methods above apply.

Two cautions. First, a transformation changes the error structure along with the mean: if $y=\beta_0e^{\beta_1x}\varepsilon$ with a multiplicative error $\varepsilon$, then $\ln y$ has an additive error and the log-linear fit is correct; if the original error is additive the log-transformed errors are not constant-variance. Always re-check the residuals after transforming. Second, predictions made on the transformed scale (a prediction of $\ln y$) must be back-transformed, and the back-transformed mean of $\ln y$ estimates the median of $y$, not its mean. For stabilising variance a common choice is $\sqrt y$ for counts and $\ln y$ when the standard deviation is proportional to the mean; the Box–Cox family $y^{(\lambda)}=(y^\lambda-1)/\lambda$ chooses $\lambda$ by maximum likelihood.
So far $x$ was a fixed regressor. Suppose instead that $(X,Y)$ are both random, with a bivariate normal distribution, and we are interested in their strength of linear association.
The population correlation is $\rho=\dfrac{\Cov(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\in[-1,1]$. For a sample the sample correlation coefficient is
R=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}=\hat\beta_1\sqrt{\frac{S_{xx}}{S_{yy}}}.

Relations: $R^2$ (the square of $R$) equals the coefficient of determination of Section 5.8.2; $R$ has the same sign as $\hat\beta_1$; $R=\pm1$ if and only if all points lie exactly on a line; and $\hat\beta_1=R\,s_y/s_x$.
If $(X,Y)$ is bivariate normal:
to test $H_0:\rho=0$ use $T_0=\dfrac{R\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-R^2}}\sim t_{n-2}$ under $H_0$ (identical to the $t$-test of $H_0:\beta_1=0$);

for other hypotheses and intervals use Fisher’s transformation: $Z=\tfrac12\ln\dfrac{1+R}{1-R}=\operatorname{arctanh}R$ is approximately $\Normal\Big(\operatorname{arctanh}\rho,\ \dfrac1{n-3}\Big)$. A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval for $\rho$ is $\tanh\big(\operatorname{arctanh}r\pm z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{n-3}\big)$.

For the example data $r=\sqrt{0.9988}=0.9994$; $t_0=0.9994\sqrt6/\sqrt{1-0.9988}=70.7$ (equals the regression $t$ up to rounding). For an interval with $n=20$ and $r=0.6$: $\operatorname{arctanh}0.6=0.693$, so $0.693\pm1.96/\sqrt{17}=0.693\pm0.475$, and $\rho\in(\tanh0.218,\tanh1.168)=(0.21,0.82)$.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Textbook example: wire bond pull strength versus wire length

blocks.x: For $n=25$ bonds, $S_{xx}=698.56$ and $S_{xy}=2027.7132$ give $r=0.9818$ and $r^2=0.9640$ (96.4% of the variability in pull strength is explained by wire length). To test $H_0:\rho=0$ at $\alpha=0.05$: $t_0=r\sqrt{23}/\sqrt{1-r^2}\approx24.8>t_{0.025,23}=2.069$, so reject. For $H_0:\rho=\rho_0$ ($\rho_0\ne0$) and moderately large samples ($n\ge25$) use $z_0=(\operatorname{arctanh}r-\operatorname{arctanh}\rho_0)\sqrt{n-3}$, rejecting for $\abs{z_0}>z_{\alpha/2}$ (or $z_\alpha$ one-sided). Here $\operatorname{arctanh}0.9818=2.3452$ and the $95\%$ interval is $\tanh(2.3452\pm1.96/\sqrt{22})=\tanh(1.927,\,2.763)$, i.e. $0.958\le\rho\le0.992$. A one-sided $95\%$ lower bound uses $z_{0.05}=1.645$ instead of $1.96$.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: correlation is not causation, and zero correlation is not independence

blocks.x: A high correlation can come from a common cause or pure coincidence. Correlation measures linear association only: $Y=X^2$ with $X$ symmetric about zero has $\rho=0$ yet $Y$ is a deterministic function of $X$. And a single outlier can create or destroy a large correlation; always look at the scatter plot (Anscombe’s quartet has four very different data sets with identical $r=0.816$ and identical regression lines).

Model $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2)$. Least squares: $\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}$, $\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}-\hat\beta_1\bar{x}$, $\hat\sigma^2=SS_E/(n-2)$ with $SS_E=S_{yy}-\hat\beta_1S_{xy}$.
$\Var[\hat\beta_1]=\sigma^2/S_{xx}$, $\Var[\hat\beta_0]=\sigma^2(1/n+\bar{x}^2/S_{xx})$; $\hat\beta$’s are BLUE (Gauss–Markov).
Tests and intervals use $t_{n-2}$; $H_0:\beta_1=0$ is also tested by $F_0=MS_R/MS_E=t_0^2$ with $SS_T=SS_R+SS_E$.
Mean response: $\hat{y}_0\pm t\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2[1/n+(x_0-\bar{x})^2/S_{xx}]}$; new observation: add $1$ inside the bracket; both are narrowest at $\bar{x}$.
Check the residuals (normal plot, versus $\hat{y}$); $R^2=SS_R/SS_T$; lack of fit needs replicates; transformations linearise some nonlinear models.
$r=S_{xy}/\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}$, $t_0=r\sqrt{n-2}/\sqrt{1-r^2}$; Fisher’s $z$ gives intervals for $\rho$.

For the data $x$: $2,4,5,7,9,10$ and $y$: $5.1,8.3,9.8,14.2,18.0,19.6$, find the least squares line, $\hat\sigma^2$, the $95\%$ confidence interval for the slope, and test $H_0:\beta_1=2$ against $\beta_1\ne2$.
Construct the analysis of variance table for the data of Exercise 1 and test the significance of regression with $\alpha=0.05$. Verify $F_0=t_0^2$ and compute $R^2$.

Using Exercise 1, find a $95\%$ confidence interval on the mean response at $x_0=6$ and a $95\%$ prediction interval for a new observation at $x_0=6$. Why is the second wider? What happens at $x_0=20$?
Prove that the residuals of a least squares line with an intercept satisfy $\sum e_i=0$ and $\sum x_ie_i=0$, and deduce that the fitted line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$.
Show that $\hat\beta_1=R\,s_y/s_x$ and $R^2=SS_R/SS_T$. If $R=0.8$ and $s_y=10$, $s_x=2$, find $\hat\beta_1$ and the proportion of variance explained.
The data below follow an approximate relationship $y=\beta_0e^{\beta_1x}$: $x=1,2,3,4,5$; $y=2.7,7.1,20.5,54.9,148.0$. Linearise, fit by least squares and estimate $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$.
In a sample of $n=27$ pairs $r=-0.45$. Test $H_0:\rho=0$ and find a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\rho$ using Fisher’s transformation.
Explain, with the help of a residual plot sketch, how to recognise (a) a nonlinear relationship, (b) non-constant variance and (c) a single outlier, and what you would do about each.
